entry.title: .tar.gz Files Cannot Be Concatenated Using Cat
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | alexwlchan.net | discussion | hacker news

The inclusion of an end-of-file (EOF) marker in the tar format prevents users from successfully concatenating .tar.gz archives using the `cat` command. While gzip is a stream compressor that allows concatenated members to be read as a single continuous stream, tar readers stop at the first EOF marker—consisting of zeroed blocks—and ignore any subsequent data.

This behavior is a legacy of tar's design for sequential access on magnetic tape. To correctly combine multiple compressed archives, the individual members must be extracted and then written into a new, single archive to ensure a single, valid EOF marker is placed at the end.

entry.title: C++26 Makes Trivial Infinite Loops Well-Defined
entry.content:
Lobsters Top | sandordargo.com | source | discussion

C++26 changes the status of trivial infinite loops, such as `while (true);`, from undefined behavior to well-defined behavior via proposal P2809R3. Previously, compilers were permitted to assume these loops would eventually terminate, which allowed them to optimize the loops away entirely. This behavior caused significant issues in embedded and kernel programming, where empty loops are often used to halt a system after a fatal error.

The standard defines a trivial infinite loop as a trivially empty iteration statement with a constant expression that evaluates to true. Under the new rules, these loops are treated as a call to `std::this_thread::yield()` to ensure forward progress. Because the proposal was also accepted as a defect report, implementations may apply this fix to earlier C++ modes as well.

entry.content:

Rust's `dyn Any` mechanism currently prevents downcasting to unsized types like `str` because the compiler-generated vtable strips pointer metadata, such as slice length. This occurs because the `DispatchFromDyn` trait discards metadata during coercion, making it impossible to reconstruct a fat pointer for types whose size is only known at runtime.

A manual vtable construction method using `unsafe` code can preserve pointer metadata on the stack to allow for the recovery of unsized types. However, this approach requires precise lifetime management and suggests that adding lifetimes to `dyn` object declarations could provide a more robust, native solution.

entry.content:

The ud2 instruction is an architecturally undefined x86 instruction designed to trigger an "invalid opcode" exception. Compilers use it to mark unreachable code, ensuring that if execution flow erroneously reaches such a point, the program crashes immediately rather than executing unintended instructions.

The instruction's name is a result of the retroactive naming of previous, unofficial methods used to trigger the exception. Developers previously relied on the 0F FF and 0F B9 byte sequences to force invalid opcodes; as Intel formalized these behaviors, the 0F FF and 0F B9 sequences were designated ud0 and ud1, respectively, leaving ud2 as the standard, parameter-free instruction.

Rust is stabilizing its "never" type (`!`), which represents values that can never occur or functions that never return. The feature enables more efficient generic code by allowing the compiler to optimize away unreachable error branches in infallible conversions and simplifies type inference for expressions like infinite loops. As part of this update, the standard library's `Infallible` type will become a type alias for the never type.

The change introduces a breaking change in how the compiler handles type inference fallback, shifting the default from the unit type `()` to `!`. While this could impact several thousand crates, many have already been addressed through community patches or backports discovered using the `crater` tool. Developers can resolve potential compilation errors by explicitly specifying return types or updating to supported dependency versions.
